FROM: Mr. Clint Shealy, Assistant City Manager, Columbia Water

DATE: September 15, 2026
Subject: Recommendation for Approval
Blanchard Sole Source Purchase Order
The Department of Procurement and Contracts in coordination with Columbia Water respectfully request
your review and approval of this Blanchard Purchase Order request from the Metro Wastewater Treatment
Plant Division. Blanchard is the authorized Caterpillar dealership in South Carolina and maintains the
warranty for the Caterpillar Generator being upgraded.
The Purchase Order amount is $282,908.42. This request is to fund the upgrade of the Caterpillar Generator
Control Panel, Switchgear, and needed auxiliary equipment for the existing onsite generator. The existing
unit is obsolete and no longer supported for service and repair.
The purpose of this procurement is to cover the manufacturer expenses for the rehab of an existing generator
and extended the useful life of that equipment with reliable controls and electrical components to minimize
failure or downtime should the generator unit be needed. This action is being taken as a proactive measure
to ensure that this lift station maintains its functionality and backup power by the most reliable means
possible and that the equipment being utilized is not the single point of potential failure. This lift station
pumps a significant amount of sanitary wastewater daily. A power failure without reliable backup power
has the potential to cause significant environmental impacts locally; this action is a set to avoid that failure.
If you have questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact our office.

RE:
Recommendation for Approval: OSHA Required Medium Voltage Testing
The Canal Water Treatment Plant respectfully requests approval to expend $91,999.80 for
comprehensive medium voltage electrical testing of the facility's electrical distribution system.
Funding for this repair will be provided through the Columbia Canal Water Treatment Plant’s
Operations and Maintenance budget.
This testing is required on a three-year maintenance cycle to ensure the continued safe and reliable
operation of the City's drinking water infrastructure and to meet OSHA requirements.
The Canal Water Treatment Plants ability to continuously operate depends on the reliability of its
medium voltage electrical distribution system, which supplies power to high-service pumps, raw
water pumps, treatment equipment, chemical feed systems, and other essential infrastructure.
Medium voltage electrical equipment naturally deteriorates over time due to age, heat, vibration,
moisture, and repeated electrical loading. Without periodic diagnostic testing and preventative
maintenance, electrical failures can occur with little or no warning. A failure of a major electrical
component has the potential to shut down significant portions of the treatment process, resulting in
costly emergency repairs, extended service interruptions, and potential impacts to the City's ability
to provide safe drinking water.
This testing is not simply a maintenance preference; it is a critical safety measure that helps ensure
compliance with applicable OSHA electrical safety requirements and recognized industry standards
for the maintenance of electrical power distribution systems. The testing identifies deteriorating
insulation, loose electrical connections, failing protective relays, transformer deficiencies, circuit
breaker problems, and other hidden defects before they develop into catastrophic equipment failures
or serious employee safety hazards.
ColumbiaSCWater.Net
The proposed testing includes specialized inspections and diagnostics that cannot be performed by
plant personnel. The work requires certified technicians using highly specialized equipment to
evaluate the condition and performance of medium voltage electrical assets while verifying that
protective devices operate correctly during electrical fault conditions.
Approving this expenditure provides several important benefits to the City:
• Protects employee safety by identifying electrical hazards before they result in arc flash
events or equipment failures.
• Reduces the likelihood of unexpected plant shutdowns and emergency repairs.
• Extends the service life of existing electrical infrastructure through preventative
maintenance.
• Verifies that protective devices operate correctly, minimizing damage during electrical
faults.
• Helps maintain uninterrupted production of safe drinking water for Columbia's customers.
• Reduces long-term maintenance costs by identifying problems early, before they require
major capital replacement.
• Demonstrates the City's commitment to regulatory compliance, sound asset management,
and responsible stewardship of public infrastructure.
The Canal Water Treatment Plant has a responsibility to maintain reliable operation of one of the
City's most critical public utilities. Investing in routine medium voltage testing is a prudent and
fiscally responsible measure that protects employees, preserves critical infrastructure, minimizes
operational risk, and ensures the continued delivery of safe, reliable drinking water to the citizens of
Columbia.
For these reasons, we respectfully request City Council's approval of the $91,999.80 expenditure for
the scheduled three-year medium voltage electrical testing program at the Canal Water Treatment
Plant.
Thank you for your consideration and support of this critical infrastructure need.

FROM: Mr. Clint Shealy, Assistant City Manager, Columbia Water

RE: Recommendation for Approval: De-Energized Electrical Testing – Phase 2
Summary:
To ensure the continued safe and reliable operation of electrical systems critical to the Lake Murray
Water Treatment Plant, Columbia Water respectfully requests City Council approval to proceed
with Phase 2 of the De-Energized Electrical Testing program.
Scope of Services:
The testing will be performed by Transworld Inc. Electric, a firm specializing in electrical
reliability testing in accordance with National Electrical Testing Association (NETA) standards.
The work will include:
• De-energized testing of medium voltage equipment.
• Inspection and verification of protective relay and trip unit settings.
• Coordination of safe system shutdowns and lockout/tagout procedures.
• Documentation of findings and recommendations for corrective actions if needed.
This testing is part of a multi-phase effort to evaluate and maintain the integrity of the electrical
distribution system at the Lake Murray Water Treatment Plant.
Procurement Details:
• Vendor: Transworld Inc. Electric
• Requisition Number: R240643
• Phase 2 Cost: $54,351.00
• Future Phases: Additional phases will be planned and budgeted in subsequent fiscal years.
ColumbiaSCWater.Net
Budget Allocation:
Funding for Phase 2 is included in the FY25-26 operational budget for Columbia Water.
Justification:
De-Energized Electrical Testing is essential for:
• Preventing costly equipment failures and unplanned outages.
• Ensuring compliance with safety and electrical reliability standards.
• Supporting uninterrupted operation of the Lake Murray Water Treatment Plant, which is
vital to the City’s water supply.
Recommendation:
Columbia Water respectfully requests City Council approval to proceed with Phase 2 of the De-
Energized Electrical Testing program with Transworld Inc. Electric in the amount of $54,351.00.

MEMORANDUM
Honorable Daniel J. Rickenmann, Mayor and Members of City Council
To: Ms. Teresa Wilson, City Manager
From: W.H. Holbrook, Chief of Police
Ms. Shannon Lizewski, Director of Procurement and Contracts
Date: June 16, 2026
Re: City Detect – R240690
The Columbia Police Department respectfully requests approval for R240690 – City Detect, in
the amount of $66,960, to be funded out of 1012402-636600
During the pilot period, City Detect demonstrated its value as a technology tool that assists Code
Enforcement personnel in identifying, documenting, and prioritizing property maintenance
concerns throughout the city. The platform utilizes image-based data collection and analysis to
provide timely information regarding property conditions, allowing staff to more efficiently identify
potential code violations, monitor neighborhood conditions, and address signs of urban blight.
By providing current visual data and analytical tools, City Detect enables Code Enforcement
personnel to proactively identify issues that may otherwise go unnoticed until citizen complaints
are received. This approach supports earlier intervention, more efficient deployment of
resources, and improved responsiveness to community concerns.
The platform is specifically utilized to support real property analysis and neighborhood
improvement efforts. Benefits include improved identification of deteriorating structures,
overgrown lots, illegal dumping, and other conditions that negatively impact neighborhood
appearance, property values, and quality of life. The technology assists staff in making informed
decisions while creating a more consistent and data-driven approach to code enforcement
activities.

RE:
Recommendation for Approval: Repair of Harden St. Pump Station Pump #2 – Columbia
Canal Water Treatment Plant - Distribution System Requisition No. R238941
The rotating assembly for Pump No. 2 at the Harden Street Pump Station requires immediate
replacement due to severe mechanical damage. This pump station is one of the City’s most critical
facilities, and continued reliable operation is essential to maintaining adequate water supply.
Inspection has confirmed that the pump’s impeller is cracked and significantly damaged, rendering
the unit unreliable for continued service. The pump was originally installed in 1968 and has been in
continuous operation since that time. The manufacturer no longer produces this model, and a full
replacement is not feasible because no modern pumps match the existing dimensions of the
installation. As a result, repair of the rotating assembly is the only viable option.
The Harden Street Pump Station requires three pumps to operate daily, and the station is equipped
with only four total pumps. With Pump No. 2 compromised, the system is operating with minimal
redundancy. If another pump were to fail before repairs are completed, the City could be forced to
reduce water supply capacity, creating a significant operational risk.
While a capital improvement project is scheduled in approximately one year to fully replace the
pump station and its equipment, the current condition of Pump No. 2 cannot wait until that time.
Immediate repair is necessary to maintain system reliability and protect against potential service
disruptions.
For these reasons, prompt approval and action are requested to proceed with the repair of the
rotating assembly for Harden Street Pump No. 2.

Approval of this repair is recommended to ensure continued operational reliability in the
Columbia Canal Water Treatment Plants distribution area and to safeguard the City’s drinking
water infrastructure.
